en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
The Chapter on the Painted Hall, 45.
The Training Rule on Legal Issues:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhunī approached the bhikkhunī Thullanandā and said to her,
“Come, noble lady, settle this legal case.
The bhikkhunī Thullanandā—
Having assented by saying, “Very well,” she neither pacified the matter nor made an effort to pacify it.
Then that bhikkhunī informed the bhikkhunīs of this matter.
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires... [as before]... were indignant, disparaged her, and complained, saying:
“How indeed could the noble lady Thullanandā, when addressed by a bhikkhunī,
‘Come, noble lady, settle this legal issue,’ and having consented by saying ‘Very well,’ neither settle it nor make an effort to settle it? …pe…
“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā, when addressed by another nun,
‘Come, noble lady, settle this legal issue,’ and having replied,
‘Very well,’ neither settles it nor makes an effort to settle it?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked her:
“… How can the bhikkhunī Thullanandā [act] toward a bhikkhunī—”
‘Come, venerable lady, settle this legal issue,’ being thus addressed, she says, ‘Very well,’ yet neither settles it nor makes an effort to settle it.
This, monks, does not lead to the inspiration of those without faith... [and so on].”
And thus, monks, let the nuns recite this training rule: “If a nun,

being addressed by another nun with the words, ‘Come, noble lady, settle this legal issue,’ and having agreed by saying ‘Very well,’ subsequently neither settles it nor makes an effort to settle it, even though she is not hindered, it is an offense entailing expiation.”
"But whichever" means whichever such...
"nun" means... [as before].
...pe... this is the nun intended in this context.
"Of a nun" means: of another nun.

A legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) refers to the four types of legal issues: a legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), a legal issue arising from an accusation (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), and a legal issue arising from business (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).
"Venerable lady, please settle this legal issue."
"Venerable lady, settle this legal issue.
"She will do so afterwards without hindrance" means:
provided there is no obstacle.
"Neither would he pacify it himself" means he would not personally pacify it.
"Nor would he make an effort for its pacification" means...
One should not command another.
Merely by laying down the burden with the thought, "I will neither settle this matter nor make an effort to settle it," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one perceives a person as fully ordained when they are indeed fully ordained, and neither settles the legal issue (adhikaraṇa) nor makes an effort to settle it, there is an offense of expiation.
If one is in doubt as to whether a person is fully ordained, and neither settles the legal issue nor makes an effort to settle it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one perceives a fully ordained person as not fully ordained, and neither settles the legal issue nor makes an effort to settle it, there is an offense of expiation.
If one neither settles a legal issue concerning a person who is not fully ordained nor makes an effort to settle it, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
If she perceives one who is not fully ordained as being fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she is doubtful regarding one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she perceives one who is not fully ordained as being not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if there is an obstacle, or if,
having searched, one does not obtain it.
For one who is ill,
in cases of emergency,
for one who is insane,
"Regarding the first offender":
thus ends the fifth training rule.
